title: Protection-Setting Mismatch During Feeder Restoration on Synthetic Meridian Loop

core_units.text: A downed conductor on the Synthetic Meridian Loop feeder left the entire branch de-energized for nineteen minutes before crews arrived.
The Synthetic Meridian Loop relay group retained a ground overcurrent pickup of 240 primary amperes from the prior seasonal configuration.
Restoration switching closed the loop backfeed path while the legacy pickup threshold remained active on the relay group.
A separate commissioning record showed the feeder had been retuned for 180 amperes during the spring load transfer, but the field relay was never updated.
Backfeed inrush from the Synthetic Meridian Loop warehouse transformer bank exceeded the legacy pickup within two cycles of the closing operation.
The relay group tripped the loop breaker, and the restoration attempt failed before any customer load was picked up.
Synthetic Meridian Loop operators re-energized the feeder from the alternate source after manually blocking the ground element.
The independent channel named Synthetic Channel Bravo recorded a peak of 268 amperes during the failed restoration attempt.
Controller-indicated current at the moment of trip read 241 amperes, while the independent channel showed 268 amperes, a 27-ampere discrepancy.
A field crew later confirmed the relay file dated from the prior autumn and had not been synchronized with the spring commissioning record.
The restoration sequence was delayed by 41 minutes while the protection engineer reviewed the relay settings against the commissioning sheet.
The protection engineer revised the ground overcurrent pickup to 180 primary amperes and pushed the updated file to the relay group.
A second restoration attempt succeeded at 14:03:12, with the independent channel showing a peak of 142 amperes, below the revised pickup.
The warehouse transformer bank was not the cause of the miscoordination; its inrush was within the expected range for a cold load pickup.
Synthetic Meridian Loop supervisory control logged the breaker trip 0.8 seconds after the restoration close command was issued.
The miscoordination exposed a gap between the seasonal relay review cycle and the field commissioning workflow for the Synthetic Meridian Loop feeder.
A temporary hold was placed on all feeder restorations on Synthetic Meridian Loop until the relay file audit was completed.
The relay group's event report captured 268 amperes on the independent channel and 241 amperes on the controller-indicated path.
The feeder restoration was ultimately completed 63 minutes after the initial downed conductor was reported.
A contributing condition was the absence of an automatic settings comparison between the relay file and the commissioning record.
The trigger for the event was the closing of the loop backfeed path while the legacy pickup threshold remained active.
The corrective action included a relay file audit and a revised pickup setting of 180 primary amperes.
The independent channel named Synthetic Channel Bravo was the only measurement source that captured the full inrush waveform.
The root cause was the mismatch between the 240-ampere legacy pickup and the 180-ampere commissioning value.
The impact was a failed restoration attempt and a 41-minute delay before the feeder was successfully re-energized.
The mitigation was the revision of the ground overcurrent pickup to 180 primary amperes and the subsequent successful restoration.

core_units.text: Synthetic Ridgeline plant recorded a measured bus voltage sag to 71 percent for 420 milliseconds on the independent channel.

A contributing condition was elevated ambient temperature raising winding resistance above the nominal threshold.
A second contributing condition was a stale capacitor bank drawing reactive power beyond its rated capacity.
The negated non-cause was a firmware update at Synthetic Ridgeline inverter, which showed no timing correlation to the event.

No permanent equipment damage was recorded at Synthetic Ridgeline plant, though thermal cycling stress was noted.
The corrective action was resetting the Synthetic Ridgeline capacitor bank and verifying its reactive draw to rated values.

title: Reserve Activation Delay Traced to Stale Telemetry Buffer at Synthetic Ridgeway Control Hub

core_units.text: At 14:03:12 the Synthetic Ridgeway hub issued a reserve activation command, and the field relay acknowledged receipt 0.4 seconds later.
The independent audit channel, Synthetic Kestrel, recorded the same command 0.3 seconds after issuance, confirming the order left the hub promptly.
Operators had scheduled a firmware refresh for the telemetry buffer at 13:40, but the refresh stalled when a checksum comparison returned mismatched values.
The stalled refresh left the buffer holding readings from 13:38, so every subsequent sample carried a timestamp nearly 25 minutes old.
A contributing condition was the buffer's 30-minute retention window, which allowed stale entries to persist well past their useful life.
A second contributing condition was the relay's polling interval of 12 seconds, which delayed detection of the stale timestamp by up to four cycles.
The stale buffer fed the hub a voltage reading of 13.7 kilovolts while the actual line held 14.1 kilovolts, a 0.4 kilovolt gap.
Because the indicated voltage sat below the 13.9 kilovolt threshold, the hub withheld the activation signal for 47 seconds.
During that hold, the relay continued polling every 12 seconds, and each poll returned the same stale 13.7 kilovolt figure.
A watchdog process flagged the timestamp skew at 14:04:01, but its alert routed to a queue that operators check only hourly.
The independent Synthetic Kestrel channel showed the line at 14.1 kilovolts throughout, a reading the hub never consulted.
Reserve delivery finally began 47 seconds after the command, and the 12 megawatt obligation was met 51 seconds late.
The delay exposed a 0.9 megawatt shortfall against the 12 megawatt commitment during the first minute of the activation window.
Synthetic Ridgeway logged the event as a 47-second response deviation, its first such deviation in 14 months of reserve tests.
No equipment tripped and no load was shed, so the impact remained confined to the response-time obligation.
Engineers restarted the telemetry buffer at 14:06:20, which cleared the stale entries and restored live timestamps.
The corrective action was to add a timestamp-freshness gate that rejects any sample older than 60 seconds before it reaches the hub.
Operators also shortened the watchdog alert queue check from hourly to every 10 minutes, closing the detection gap.
A post-event replay confirmed the hub would have activated on time had it used the Synthetic Kestrel reading instead of the buffer.
The firmware checksum mismatch was not caused by the relay polling interval, which functioned within its 12-second specification.
